name: Community Forensics
maintainer: Jeongsoo Park / Owens Lab (University of Michigan)
purpose: Synthetic-image detector trained on a dataset assembled from thousands of community-published generative models, aimed at generalising beyond the handful of generators most detectors see.
journalism_use_case: The most defensible currently available open detector baseline for 'is this image synthetic?' triage, because its training distribution covers thousands of generators rather than a handful — still a lead generator for reporting, not an adjudicator.
pros: Training-distribution breadth is the right response to the generalisation problem that defeats most detectors — thousands of generators rather than a curated few
MIT code and MIT weights (stated on the OwensLab/commfor-model-384 HuggingFace model card), so it is commercially usable without licence review
Inference runs locally after download, so case images need not be sent to a detection service
Recent enough (pushed 2026-01-06) to cover a meaningful span of modern generators
cons: Output is a probability — an assistive signal that cannot establish whether an image was AI-generated, and is not conclusive proof
The repository does not document accuracy bounds, calibration or per-generator performance, so you cannot state an error rate when an editor asks for one
Low activity and tiny community (64 stars, 2 open issues, no releases) — you would own any maintenance
Weights and datasets are fetched from HuggingFace and Dropbox-hosted checkpoints, which is a supply-chain and availability risk
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: MIT weights stated on the OwensLab/commfor-model-384 HuggingFace card (read session 1, retained); 64 stars; no documented calibration in the repository, which is itself the significant gap.
assessment: If you must have an open synthetic-image detector, this is the one I would use, because the training breadth is the only property that correlates with real-world performance and the licence is clean. But I would deploy it with an explicit internal policy: the score goes in the reporting notes, never in the story, and a synthetic-media claim requires non-forensic corroboration. The absence of documented calibration means you cannot honestly publish a confidence figure derived from it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-01-06, no releases or tags, 64 stars, 2 open issues. Ten months since last push; an academic release that appears complete rather than abandoned, but with no evidence of ongoing work.
model_or_data_licence: MIT, stated on the OwensLab/commfor-model-384 HuggingFace model card.
licence_restrictions: None material — unusually clean for a forensic model. The training dataset aggregates outputs from many third-party generators, whose own terms are a residual consideration if you redistribute the dataset.
costs: No fee. GPU for practical inference throughput; weight and dataset downloads from HuggingFace and Dropbox. Estimate.
privacy: Weights and datasets fetched from HuggingFace and Dropbox; after download, inference runs locally so case images need not leave your infrastructure.
alternatives: UniversalFakeDetect as a second baseline for comparison
Deepfake-Eval-2024 for the in-the-wild degradation figures that contextualise any score
Provenance-based verification (C2PA, reverse search, source contact) which is more reliable than detection

name: Noiseprint
purpose: CNN that extracts a camera-model noise fingerprint from an image, enabling detection of regions whose fingerprint differs from the rest of the frame or from a claimed camera model.
journalism_use_case: Testing whether a photo's noise fingerprint is consistent with the camera model it is claimed to come from, or whether part of the frame carries a different fingerprint from the rest — a splicing indicator independent of JPEG block artefacts, which makes it a genuinely complementary second opinion to CAT-Net.
pros: Provides a signal independent of compression artefacts, so it can corroborate or contradict JPEG-based methods rather than merely repeating them
Camera-model consistency testing addresses a specific, answerable question ('is this from the device claimed?') rather than a vague authenticity score
Local inference with author-provided weights, no third-party service documented
cons: NOT open source: LICENSE.txt restricts use to informational and non-profit purposes, copyright GRIP-UNINA — the same restriction as TruFor and a blocker for commercial newsroom use
TensorFlow 1.2.1 pin makes installation genuinely painful in 2026; you will fight the environment before you see a result
Open PR backlog and limited maintenance (pushed 2026-03-27, no releases, 158 stars, 16 open issues)
Noise fingerprints are destroyed by resizing and platform recompression, so the method applies only to images close to original — a narrow slice of real cases
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the LICENSE.txt restriction to informational and non-profit use (read session 1, retained); the TensorFlow 1.2.1 pin stated in the repository; 16 open issues including an open PR backlog.
assessment: Specialist, legally restricted and operationally awkward — I would not deploy it in a commercial newsroom. Where it genuinely helps is in partnership with an academic forensics group, which is also the context its licence contemplates. For your profile the actionable alternative is to build the camera-consistency check differently: ExifTool plus MediaInfo for declared device metadata, CAT-Net for compression-based splicing, and an expert partner when a case warrants PRNU-class analysis.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-03-27, no releases or tags, 158 stars, 16 open issues including unmerged PRs. Eight months since last push, a long-obsolete framework pin, and unaddressed contributions — declining rather than merely low-activity.
licence: NOT OSS — custom GRIP-UNINA terms: LICENSE.txt restricts use to informational and non-profit purposes
licence_restrictions: Commercial use not permitted without separate permission; redistribution restricted. Do not assume a commercially published investigation is 'informational' use.
costs: No fee for permitted use. Hidden cost is the environment: a TensorFlow 1.2.1 pin realistically means a dedicated container and hours of engineer time.
privacy: Local inference, no third-party service documented. Suitable for sensitive images on an isolated machine, if you can get it running.
alternatives: CAT-Net for commercially usable splicing detection
TruFor for stronger localisation if non-profit use applies
Collaboration with an academic image-forensics group for PRNU-class camera analysis

name: x-ray
purpose: Python library that inspects PDFs for bad redactions — text that remains in the content stream beneath a drawn black rectangle — and reports the recoverable text.
journalism_use_case: Triaging FOIA releases, court filings and leaked document sets for failed redactions that reveal names, figures or passages the releasing body intended to withhold. This is a recurring source of scoops, and also the routine check you run before relying on a document being genuinely redacted.
pros: Automates a check that is otherwise accidental: failed redactions are found when someone happens to copy-paste, and x-ray turns that into a systematic sweep over thousands of documents
Built by Free Law Project against a very large corpus of real court filings, so the heuristics are tuned on the documents that actually exhibit the failure
BSD-2-Clause, pure Python, fully local — appropriate for sensitive leaked documents
Dual value: offensive (find what others hid) and defensive (check your own publications before release)
cons: Detection is heuristic: outputs are candidate bad redactions, not conclusive findings, and both false positives and missed redactions occur
Finds text-layer failures only — an image-based redaction that is merely a low-opacity overlay, or a scan of a poorly redacted page, is outside its scope
GitHub release metadata lags the tag line (release v0.3.5 from 2025-12-08 versus tag v0.4.0), so pinning requires care
44 open issues against 837 stars with a small maintainer team
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. The institutional context is strong and checkable: Free Law Project operates CourtListener over millions of filings and built x-ray for that corpus, which is credible production provenance. Failed redactions in court and government documents are a well-documented recurring phenomenon.
assessment: Adopt it twice over: as a sweep on every document set you receive, and as a mandatory pre-publication check on every document you release. The second use is the one newsrooms skip and the one that protects sources — publishing a 'redacted' PDF whose text layer is intact has burned sources before. Pair it with PyMuPDF for applying true redactions, and remember x-ray cannot see image-based failures, so visual spot-checks remain necessary.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v0.3.5 (2025-12-08), latest tag v0.4.0, 837 stars, 44 open issues. Current commits with a tag ahead of the published release; maintained by a functioning non-profit that uses it operationally.
costs: No fee, negligible compute. No paid dependencies.
privacy: Local processing with no third-party service — essential, since the documents you run it over are by definition ones containing information someone tried to withhold.
alternatives: kuroi for the publishing-side problem of finding and removing sensitive data at scale (LLM-based, with its own caveats)
PyMuPDF to apply genuine redactions that remove underlying text
Manual copy-paste spot checks, which x-ray systematises

name: kuroi
purpose: CLI tool that uses an LLM backend to identify personal and source-identifying information in documents at scale, so it can be redacted before publication.
journalism_use_case: The publishing-side counterpart to x-ray: before an investigative team releases primary-source documents, use it to find source-identifying and personal data across thousands of pages rather than redacting page by page — the step that makes large document releases feasible without burning sources.
pros: Addresses a real bottleneck: manual redaction is why many newsrooms publish three documents instead of three hundred, and automating the detection stage changes what is publishable
Built by ICIJ for its own large-scale document releases, which is the most relevant provenance possible for this task
Recent and released (v0.1.3, 2026-10-13) under AGPL-3.0
Backend-agnostic in principle, so it can be pointed at a self-hosted model
cons: LLM-based detection of sensitive data is probabilistic, NOT conclusive — it will miss identifiers and flag non-sensitive text, so output must be human-reviewed before any release, and treating it as complete would be dangerous
CRITICAL privacy issue: if configured against a hosted LLM, the sensitive document content being redacted is sent to that provider — the exact material you are trying to protect
Very low adoption (6 stars, 0 open issues) and version 0.1.x — early software for a high-stakes task
AGPL-3.0 affects redistribution of modified network services built around it
feedback: No individual user reports verified — 6 stars means there is no community signal, which I state rather than embellish. The ICIJ provenance is the substantive evidence; the hosted-LLM exposure risk is inherent to the architecture and is flagged in this catalogue rather than reported by users.
assessment: Conceptually the right tool for a real problem, and I would pilot it — but only against a self-hosted model, never a hosted API. The irony is sharp: a tool for protecting sources that, misconfigured, transmits unredacted source documents to a third party. For your profile the deployment shape is: local LLM (via vLLM or llama.cpp), kuroi for candidate detection, human review of every candidate, PyMuPDF for the actual redaction, then x-ray as a verification sweep before release. That chain is genuinely useful; any link using a hosted model is not.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-13, latest release v0.1.3 published the same day, 6 stars, 0 open issues. Recent release from an institutional maintainer; early-stage but current. Low adoption means little external testing.
model_or_data_licence: n/a — depends on whichever LLM the operator configures; that model's licence and the provider's terms apply.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: modified network-service redistribution triggers source-release obligations. Internal use unaffected.
costs: Software free. Cost depends entirely on the LLM backend: a self-hosted model means GPU infrastructure; a hosted model means per-token charges (not priced here) plus an unacceptable disclosure. Human review time remains the dominant cost and is not reduced to zero.
privacy: Depends on configuration and the difference is total. Self-hosted LLM: fully local and appropriate. Hosted LLM: the unredacted sensitive content is transmitted to that provider, which defeats the purpose. This must be a locked configuration, not a per-user choice.
alternatives: Presidio for rule-and-NER-based PII detection without an LLM — more predictable, less capable on unusual identifiers
x-ray for the complementary check that redactions actually removed the text
Manual redaction for small, high-stakes document sets
blockers: Hosted-LLM configuration would transmit unredacted sensitive documents to a third party — must be pinned to a self-hosted model

name: DeepfakeBench
purpose: Unified benchmark and training framework implementing many published face-manipulation detectors with standardised preprocessing, training and cross-dataset evaluation.
journalism_use_case: The practical way a technically staffed newsroom or research partner can run several published detectors over the same suspect video and see whether they agree, instead of trusting one black-box score — and the reference for how badly detectors generalise outside their training data.
pros: Standardised preprocessing and evaluation is the methodological contribution: it makes detector comparisons meaningful, where published numbers otherwise are not comparable
Implements many detectors in one framework, so an ensemble-of-opinions workflow is practical rather than a multi-week integration
The project's own framing is honest — cross-dataset generalisation remains the open problem — which is exactly the message a newsroom needs
Substantial community for a research framework (1,142 stars) with a tagged release (v1.0.3)
cons: CC-BY-NC-4.0 licence on the framework: non-commercial only, so a commercially operated newsroom cannot use it as infrastructure without permission — and GitHub reports NOASSERTION, so this is easy to miss
Benchmark datasets must be obtained separately under their own agreements, and the repository marks some as not rights-cleared — a compounding legal complication
Outputs are probabilistic scores, NEVER conclusive proof of manipulation; detectors scoring near-perfectly in-domain degrade sharply in the wild
Activity has slowed (pushed 2025-08-20, release 2024-05-27) with 101 open issues; heavy PyTorch/CUDA setup
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the CC-BY-NC-4.0 framework licence and the repository's own notes that some datasets are not rights-cleared (recorded session 1, retained); 1,142 stars with 101 open issues; last push 2025-08-20.
assessment: Use it through a research partner rather than in-house if your outlet is commercial — the NC licence plus the dataset rights questions make direct use legally untidy. Its real value to you is the published finding rather than the software: detector agreement is informative, detector scores are not, and in-the-wild performance is far below reported figures. For an editor conversation, DeepfakeBench plus Deepfake-Eval-2024 together make the case for not publishing on detector output.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-08-20, latest release v1.0.3 (2024-05-27), SPDX NOASSERTION (actual licence CC-BY-NC-4.0), 1,142 stars, 101 open issues. Fifteen months since last push and over two years since the release, with a growing backlog.
model_or_data_licence: CC-BY-NC-4.0 for the framework; per-dataset terms vary and the repository marks some datasets as not rights-cleared.
licence_restrictions: Non-commercial only — a blocker for commercially operated newsrooms. NGO or non-profit status does not automatically satisfy NonCommercial where output is commercially published. Separately, some bundled dataset references are not rights-cleared, so dataset acquisition carries its own risk.
costs: No fee for non-commercial use. Requires GPU/CUDA infrastructure and large dataset downloads obtained under separate agreements. Engineer time for setup is substantial. Estimate.
privacy: Local training and inference. Dataset acquisition involves third-party request forms and downloads, which discloses your interest to dataset custodians but not your case material.
alternatives: A research partner running it on your behalf under the NC licence
Community Forensics for an MIT-licensed single-detector baseline
Deepfake-Eval-2024 for the in-the-wild performance figures to cite
blockers: Some referenced datasets are not rights-cleared

name: FaceForensics++
purpose: Large dataset of manipulated face videos produced with several face-swap and reenactment methods at multiple compression levels, plus baseline detection code.
journalism_use_case: The canonical reference corpus behind most published face-swap detectors — useful to a newsroom's technical partner for sanity-checking any vendor-pitched detector, and to reporters as the citation for why detector accuracy figures in press materials should be distrusted.
pros: The reference dataset for the whole subfield, so understanding it is understanding what published detector numbers actually mean
Multiple compression levels included, which is what allows honest measurement of the degradation that destroys real-world detection
MIT code licence for the baseline implementations
cons: Data is released under the separate 'FaceForensics Terms of Use' — a research-oriented PDF agreement, not an SPDX open licence — and access requires completing a Google Form for approval, so it is not freely usable infrastructure

Dated relative to current generators: it predates modern diffusion and audio-driven video synthesis, so a detector trained only on FF++ transfers poorly to 2024-2026 in-the-wild fakes. Any detector claiming high FF++ accuracy has told you almost nothing
Dormant: last push 2022-12-08, 98 open issues against 2,804 stars
The access flow routes through a Google Form and the authors' email, which discloses your organisation's interest
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the separate FaceForensics Terms of Use (research-oriented agreement, not SPDX) and the Google Form access requirement; last push 2022-12-08; 2,804 stars with 98 open issues.
assessment: Reference only, and specifically useful as a rhetorical instrument: when a vendor cites FF++ performance, the correct response is that FF++ predates the generators in use today. For your profile there is no reason to obtain the dataset unless you are training detectors, which I would not recommend a newsroom do. The dataset's real contribution to your work is the argument it supports about detector limits.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2022-12-08, no releases, SPDX NOASSERTION, 2,804 stars, 98 open issues. Four years inactive with a large backlog. The dataset itself is static, so dormancy mainly affects the baseline code.
licence: MIT (code); data under the separate 'FaceForensics Terms of Use' research agreement — not an SPDX open licence
model_or_data_licence: FaceForensics Terms of Use (research-oriented PDF agreement, approval required).
licence_restrictions: Dataset access is gated and governed by a research-use agreement. Not usable as commercial infrastructure; redistribution is prohibited. Terms must be read before any use.
costs: No fee. Access requires a Google Form application and approval. Large download; GPU for any training. Estimate.
privacy: The dataset request flows through a Google Form and the authors' email, disclosing your organisation's interest; the download script pulls from the project's servers. Your own case material is not involved.
alternatives: Deepfake-Eval-2024 for in-the-wild evaluation data closer to current conditions
DeepfakeBench for a unified evaluation framework — non-commercial licence
Not training detectors at all, which is my recommendation for a newsroom
blockers: Gated research-use dataset agreement — not usable as commercial infrastructure
Predates current generative models, limiting relevance

name: SelfBlendedImages (SBI)
purpose: Face-manipulation detection method trained on synthetically self-blended images rather than on specific deepfake generators, aiming for generator-agnostic detection.
journalism_use_case: A generator-agnostic face-manipulation detector worth running as one signal in an ensemble, since it was designed for the case journalists actually face — a fake made with a tool nobody has trained on.
pros: The training approach (self-blending real faces rather than collecting generator outputs) directly targets the generalisation problem, which is the right instinct for real-world verification
Authors report honest cross-dataset figures rather than only in-domain results — roughly 93.8% AUC on Celeb-DF and 97.9% on DFD but only about 73.0% on DFDC — which is the useful disclosure
Local inference, so case material stays in the newsroom
cons: Licence is custom research-only: the authors state the code and pretrained model are 'freely available for research purpose' and commercial use requires a separate licence agreement — not usable by a commercial newsroom without permission

Probabilistic signal only, never conclusive proof of manipulation; and the authors' own spread (73.0% to 97.9% AUC depending on test set) shows how much performance depends on what the fake was made with
Pretrained weights hosted on Google Drive — availability and supply-chain risk
Low activity (pushed 2026-03-13, no releases, 277 stars, 26 open issues) and a preprocessing pipeline requiring facial landmark detection
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented from the repository: the research-only licence statement requiring a separate agreement for commercial use, and the authors' reported cross-dataset AUCs (≈93.8% Celeb-DF, ≈97.9% DFD, ≈73.0% DFDC) — these are author-reported figures, not independent measurements.
assessment: Methodologically one of the better ideas in deepfake detection and legally unavailable to a commercial newsroom. For your profile the honest conclusion across this whole subcategory is uncomfortable but important: the open detectors are either non-commercial, dormant, or demonstrably unreliable in the wild, so a newsroom's synthetic-media strategy should rest on provenance (C2PA, source contact, earliest-upload tracing) rather than detection. Keep SBI as a research-partner option.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-03-13, no releases or tags, SPDX NOASSERTION, 277 stars, 26 open issues. Eight months since last push; a complete research release with light attention.
licence: Custom research-only terms — authors state code and pretrained model are 'freely available for research purpose'; commercial use requires a separate licence agreement
model_or_data_licence: Same research-only terms apply to the pretrained model.
licence_restrictions: Commercial use prohibited without a separate agreement. A commercially published investigation is not research use.
costs: No fee for research use; commercial use requires a negotiated agreement (terms not publicly listed). GPU for inference; weights from Google Drive.
privacy: Local inference; weight download from Google Drive is the only external touchpoint. Case images stay local.
alternatives: Community Forensics for an MIT-licensed detector usable commercially
LAA-Net for compression-robust detection — also academic-licence restricted
Provenance-based verification rather than detection, which I would prioritise
blockers: Research-only licence; commercial use requires a separate agreement

name: LAA-Net
purpose: Localised artefact attention network for deepfake detection, designed to remain effective on low-quality and compressed video rather than only on pristine inputs.
journalism_use_case: A quality-agnostic detector aimed at the verification pain point most detectors fail on — compressed social-media re-uploads — making it relevant as a second or third opinion in a technical partner's detector ensemble, not as a standalone verdict tool.
pros: Explicitly targets compressed and low-quality input, which is the condition of essentially every video a journalist is asked to verify — most detectors are evaluated on pristine data and fail here
Published with cross-dataset results, so the generalisation claim can be examined rather than taken on trust
Local inference, so case video stays in the newsroom
cons: SnT Academic License: the README states the software is copyright University of Luxembourg under an academic licence (academic use only, not OSI-approved) — so it is not usable as commercial newsroom infrastructure without permission
Outputs are probabilistic signals, not conclusive proof of manipulation, and reported numbers show the familiar family-wide spread across test sets
Pinned older CUDA/PyTorch versions plus a facial alignment and landmark preprocessing chain — a painful install
Low activity (pushed 2025-11-26, no releases, 180 stars, 16 open issues)
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented from the repository README: the SnT academic licence with University of Luxembourg copyright, restricting use to academic purposes; 180 stars, 16 open issues, last push 2025-11-26.
assessment: Same pattern as SBI and TruFor: the technically interesting work in this field sits behind academic licences that a commercial newsroom cannot use. If you have a university partner, LAA-Net is worth including in their ensemble precisely because of the compression robustness. In-house, it is off the table. This recurring licence pattern is itself a finding worth carrying into your planning: the deepfake-detection field has no credible, maintained, commercially usable open option today.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-11-26, no releases or tags, SPDX NOASSERTION, 180 stars, 16 open issues. Nearly twelve months since last push; a complete academic release.
licence: SnT Academic License — README states copyright University of Luxembourg, academic use only; not OSI-approved
model_or_data_licence: Same academic licence applies to released weights.
licence_restrictions: Academic use only. Commercial newsroom use requires permission from the University of Luxembourg. Benchmark datasets are obtained separately under their own terms.
costs: No fee for academic use; commercial use requires permission (terms not publicly listed). GPU with pinned older CUDA/PyTorch; significant setup time. Estimate.
privacy: Local inference; datasets obtained separately. Case material stays local.
alternatives: A university partner running it under the academic licence
Community Forensics for commercially usable image-level detection
Provenance and earliest-upload tracing instead of detection
blockers: Academic-only licence — not usable as commercial newsroom infrastructure

name: AASIST
purpose: Graph-attention-based anti-spoofing model for speech, detecting synthetic and converted voice using integrated spectro-temporal graph attention over raw audio.
journalism_use_case: Screening suspect voice notes, leaked 'audio recordings' of politicians and robocall clips for synthesis or voice-conversion artefacts — the audio half of verification, where there is far less tooling available than for video and where fabricated audio has already been used in elections.
pros: Addresses a genuine and growing gap: synthetic audio is cheaper to produce and harder to verify than video, and there are very few open tools
MIT code with pretrained models shipped in-repository under the same licence — unusually clean licensing for this field, and the main reason to prefer it over the academic-licensed alternatives
Fully local inference with no API keys, so a suspect recording stays in the newsroom
Compact model that runs without heavy infrastructure
cons: Outputs a probabilistic spoofing score, NOT proof that audio is synthetic — and in a field where a false accusation against a politician is catastrophic, that distinction is everything
The headline sub-1% EER figures are on ASVspoof 2019 logical access, a clean studio-condition benchmark; published in-the-wild performance is far worse, so the impressive number does not transfer
Dormant: last push 2023-06-25, no releases or tags, 314 stars, 4 open issues — three years inactive, and the synthesis methods it was trained against are now superseded
Requires the ASVspoof 2019 LA dataset (separate terms) for training or re-evaluation
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: MIT licence for code and in-repo pretrained models; dormancy since June 2023; the benchmark-versus-in-the-wild performance gap, which is consistent with the Deepfake-Eval-2024 finding of roughly 48% AUC degradation for audio models moved to in-the-wild data.
assessment: The best-licensed option in a weak field, and worth having precisely because audio verification has so few alternatives — but its training predates current voice-cloning systems, so treat a negative result as nearly meaningless and a positive result as a lead. For your profile the practical posture on suspect audio is: run AASIST, run forced alignment or spectral inspection, and above all pursue provenance — who first posted it, what the earliest copy's metadata says, whether the purported speaker's circumstances fit. Detection alone should never carry a story.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2023-06-25, no releases or tags, 314 stars, 4 open issues. Three years inactive. Material here because the threat model (voice synthesis methods) has changed substantially since.
model_or_data_licence: MIT — pretrained models shipped in-repository under the same licence.
licence_restrictions: None material. The ASVspoof 2019 LA dataset used for training/evaluation has its own separate terms.
costs: No fee. Modest GPU or even CPU for inference on short clips. ASVspoof dataset obtained separately for any retraining. Estimate.
privacy: Fully local inference with no API keys — the suspect recording never leaves your machine, which matters because the audio itself may identify a source.
alternatives: ASVspoof 2021 baseline systems for the official scoring code to compute your own EER — but licence unconfirmed
Commercial audio-detection services, which upload the clip and whose accuracy claims deserve the same scepticism
Provenance investigation and spectral/forced-alignment analysis as the primary approach
blockers: Dormant since 2023; trained against pre-2024 synthesis methods

name: ASVspoof 2021 baseline systems
purpose: Reference baseline implementations and the official evaluation/scoring code for the ASVspoof 2021 anti-spoofing challenge, covering logical access, physical access and speech deepfake tracks.
journalism_use_case: The reference implementations and, more importantly, the official scoring code for audio deepfake detection — what you use to independently compute equal error rate on your own test clips rather than accepting a vendor's self-reported number.
pros: The official scoring code is the genuinely valuable artefact: it lets you measure a detector's performance on your own material with the field's standard metric, instead of trusting marketing
Covers the speech deepfake track specifically, which is the track relevant to fabricated audio of public figures
Fully local training, inference and scoring with no third-party API calls
cons: No root LICENSE file was found (a fetch of /blob/main/LICENSE returned 404), so licensing could not be confirmed and may differ per baseline subdirectory — treat reuse as legally unresolved
MATLAB is required for the GMM baselines' original versions (Python ports are provided), which is a paid dependency for part of the repository
Dormant: last push 2024-06-06, no releases, 259 stars, 16 open issues
ASVspoof evaluation data is obtained separately under its own terms, so the benchmark is not self-contained
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the absence of a root LICENSE file, verified in session 1 by a direct fetch returning 404, and retained as unresolved; the MATLAB requirement for original GMM baselines; last push 2024-06-06.
assessment: Worth knowing for one specific purpose — computing EER yourself with the standard scoring code — which is a genuinely useful capability when assessing an audio-detection vendor. But the unresolved licence means I would not vendor this code into a newsroom product; read it, reimplement the metric (EER is a short, well-specified calculation), and avoid the licence question entirely. That is my recommendation for your profile: take the methodology, not the repository.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-06-06, no releases or tags, no detected licence, 259 stars, 16 open issues. Over two years inactive; challenge-cycle repositories are typically frozen after the event.
licence: NOT CONFIRMED — no root LICENSE file found (direct fetch of /blob/main/LICENSE returned 404); terms may differ per baseline subdirectory
model_or_data_licence: Not verified. ASVspoof evaluation data is obtained separately under its own terms.
licence_restrictions: Unresolved — treat reuse and redistribution as legally unclear. Per-subdirectory licences may differ, so a blanket assumption either way is unsafe.
costs: No fee for the code. MATLAB (a paid product) is required for the original GMM baselines; Python ports avoid this. Evaluation data obtained separately. Estimate.
privacy: Local training, inference and scoring; no third-party API calls.
alternatives: Reimplementing EER yourself from the metric definition, avoiding the licence question
AASIST for an MIT-licensed detector with in-repo weights
Commissioning an independent evaluation from an academic partner
blockers: No licence file — reuse legally unresolved

name: Deepfake-Eval-2024
purpose: Benchmark of in-the-wild deepfake media collected from real circulation in 2024, with documentation and labels, used to measure how published detectors perform outside curated academic datasets.
journalism_use_case: The citation to reach for when an editor or vendor claims a detector is '98% accurate'. Its central finding is that open-source state-of-the-art detector AUC drops by roughly 50% for video, 48% for audio and 45% for image models when moved from academic benchmarks to in-the-wild media.
pros: Supplies the single most useful number in this entire subcategory for newsroom decision-making: detectors lose roughly half their apparent accuracy on real circulating media
In-the-wild collection methodology is what makes it credible where FF++ and similar curated datasets are not
